exclusions.reason: The OP performs grant-based (subject-scoped) back-channel logout and advertises backchannel_logout_session_supported: false, which is spec-legal (the OIDC Back-Channel Logout metadata is optional). This certification module unconditionally requires session_supported: true. Session-scoped sid logout is an opt-in profile planned for a future minor; sub-only logout is the fail-secure default.
Cascades from the discovery-endpoint-verification module above: the plan aborts on the session_supported assertion before this module can run. Same rationale as that exclusion.

The dynamic certification profile also requires the id_token and token id_token response types and the implicit grant, which this OP does not implement (it serves the authorization code flow only, as OAuth 2.0 Security BCP recommends). The signing-algorithm checks in this module pass when the plan runs against an RS256 OP; the remaining failures are OIDCCCheckDiscEndpointResponseTypesSupportedDynamic and OIDCCCheckDiscEndpointGrantTypesSupportedDynamic.

The module registers a client with userinfo_signed_response_alg RS256 and no userinfo encryption. Dynamic registration rejects that member with invalid_client_metadata because the OP returns the signed UserInfo shape to a request carrying Accept: application/jwt rather than to a registration value. The algorithm is not the cause: the same registration is rejected with ES256, and the OP issues RS256 UserInfo when configured with WithSigningAlgorithm(AlgRS256).

accepted_outcomes.reason: These modules assert that an RS256-signed client assertion or request object is REJECTED under a FAPI profile. The suite skips them because the client JWKS the suite registers for the FAPI plans holds only an ES256 key, so it has no RSA key to sign the negative case with. FAPI profiles refuse RS256 issuing on the OP side as well, so a skip is the correct outcome rather than a gap.

Request-object modules under the OIDC basic / formpost / dynamic plans. Those plans run op-demo in its non-FAPI profile, which does not enable JAR, so request= and request_uri= are not advertised and the suite skips the modules that would exercise them. JAR is covered by the FAPI 2.0 plans, where it is mandatory and every request-object module runs.
Same cause as the request-object family: the OIDC dynamic plan runs the non-FAPI profile, which does not advertise request_uri support.

The module asks for an unsigned (alg=none) id_token. The OP signs every id_token and does not advertise none, so the suite skips rather than running an assertion the configuration cannot reach. Refusing to issue an unsigned id_token is the intended posture, not a missing feature.

sector_identifier_uri modules under the dynamic plan. Pairwise subjects are an opt-in configuration (WithPairwiseSubject) and op-demo runs the dynamic plan with the public subject type, so the suite skips the sector-identifier tests. The pairwise path itself is covered by the library's own tests and by examples/34-pairwise-saas.

PAR request_uri refusals: reuse, expiry, and cross-client presentation. The OP correctly refuses before redirecting, so there is no callback for the suite to assert on and it asks a human to confirm the rendered error instead. The refusals themselves are pinned by the library's own tests, so the REVIEW is about the page a user sees, not about whether the refusal happened.

JAR parameter-mismatch refusals: a state or nonce that differs inside and outside the request object, or is over-long. The OP refuses before redirecting, so as with the PAR family the suite can only ask a human to confirm the rendered error page.

Long state and nonce on the authorization request. The OP accepts the long value and completes the flow: the state comes back in the authorization response and the token request succeeds. The module's ExpectRequestObjectWithLongStateErrorPage / LongNonce condition allows either an error page or a successful flow and records a review item in both cases, so the module finishes as REVIEW even when every assertion passes.
Same shape as the request-object mismatch family: a state supplied only outside the request object must be ignored, the request refused pre-redirect, and the resulting error page reviewed by a human.
An unsigned bare-wire authorization request under a FAPI 2.0 profile is refused before redirect (PAR and JAR are both mandatory there), leaving an error page for a human to confirm.

RP-Initiated Logout modules. Every one of them ends on a screen the OP renders itself — the logout confirmation prompt, or the error page for a bad id_token_hint / unregistered post_logout_redirect_uri — because a logout the OP refuses must not redirect back to the RP. The suite has no callback to assert on and asks a human to look.

logo_uri / policy_uri / tos_uri modules. The suite registers a client carrying those URIs and asks a human to confirm the consent screen presents them. Whether they render is a property of the interaction driver the embedder supplies, not of the library, so no automated assertion could stand in for the reviewer here.

Redirect-URI validation modules: unregistered, absent, or query-mismatched redirect_uri values. The OP must refuse without redirecting — sending the error to an unvalidated URI is the open-redirect the check exists to prevent — so the outcome is a rendered error page and the suite asks a human to confirm it.

An authorization request with no response_type. The module carries a mandatory 'upload a screenshot of the error page showing a missing response type error' step, so an unattended run cannot take it past REVIEW. Every other entry in the module records SUCCESS: the OP returned the error rather than a code, echoed the original state, sent a matching iss, and included no parameters beyond the expected ones. The suite sometimes concludes the module before it raises the screenshot step, which is why this same OP has recorded PASSED on some runs and REVIEW on others; admitting REVIEW is what makes the gate independent of that race, and "intermittent" is what keeps the run where it passes from reading as a stale rule.

max_age=1 must force re-authentication. The suite cannot see the OP's login screen, so it asks a human to confirm the second authorization request actually prompted rather than reusing the session. The auth_time claim that backs the decision is pinned by the library's own tests.
Same shape as max-age-1: prompt=login must re-prompt an already-authenticated browser, and only a human can confirm the login screen was shown again.

unreachable_verdicts.reason: The module asks the operator to rotate the authorization server's signing keys and then press Start. The library takes its keyset at op.New and exposes no runtime rotation API, so a deployment rotates by constructing a new provider — which the harness cannot do mid-module without dropping the in-memory store the dynamic plan's registered client lives in. Nothing about this is a defect in what the OP serves: the JWKS endpoint publishes every configured key and the kid selection is exercised by the library's own tests. It is a capability the harness cannot trigger.
unreachable_verdicts.evidence: Ran standalone against a live suite: the module logs 'Please rotate the keys on the authorization server then press the Start button' and stays CONFIGURED until the runner's idle bound. Driving Start without an actual rotation would assert nothing.

unreachable_verdicts.reason: The OP cannot fetch the request_uri the suite publishes at https://localhost.emobix.co.uk:8443: the suite's nginx serves a self-signed certificate, and op-demo installs the conformance CA only on the JWKS fetcher's transport, not on the request_uri fetcher, so /authorize answers invalid_request_uri (request_uri fetch failed) before redirecting and the suite waits for a callback that never comes. The signing algorithm is not the cause: the run against an RS256 OP fails at the fetch, before the request object is verified.
unreachable_verdicts.evidence: Re-run standalone against an RS256 op-demo: /authorize returns {"error":"invalid_request_uri","error_description":"request_uri fetch failed"}; the generic fetch failure (not the blocked-network wording) and a curl to the same URL failing certificate verification without -k place the failure in TLS trust.
